newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian unions see 7 million striking over pay.
newsitem.headline: Russian unions see 7 million striking over pay.

text.p: A top union leader said on Wednesday seven million Russians would stage a one-day protest strike next week, but the action appears to have lost some momentum since Monday's government reshuffle.
"Across all regions of Russia, unions will act," Mikhail Shmakov, head of the Federation of Independent Trade Unions, told a news conference.
But President Boris Yeltsin's surprise government reshuffle unveiled on Monday appeared to have pre-empted the union's main political demand of a new government.

Communists and their allies in the opposition had pinned hopes on the March 27 strikes as a catalyst for a new offensive against Yeltsin's government and said a no-confidence motion in parliament was possible after the protest.
Yeltsin's foe Alexander Lebed said last week that the protests could mark a decisive stage in government crisis.
Protest leaders however are now finding it harder to make the case that politicans in office less than a week should be fired for their inaction and ineptitude.

Shmakov said that only the federation's executive body could change its call for a new government, so the demand remained. But on Wednesday he sidestepped the issue and focused on the payment of back wages.

He said that 22,000 firms with seven million workers nationwide had agreed to participate in the day-long March 27 strike. He said millions of others would also take part in public demonstrations across the country of 150 million.

The government and enterprises across Russia owe their workers a total of $8 billion in back pay, Shmakov said. The average delay is now five months, but some workers had not seen a pay check in over a year, he said.
Unions are demanding payment of back wages and a change in government legal and economic policy so that such delays do not happen again in the future.
The government's new top economic official, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, said on Tuesday that broad systemic changes were needed to address the issue of unpaid salaries.
"That is a serious problem and not the kind of problem that can be solved in one week or two," he told Reuters.

"For solving that problem first we need property rights, we need to develop the securities market, to speed up the privatisation process and that is something on the agenda of the government," he said.
To a large extent Russia's back-wage crisis, which the government blames on tax-dodging, is caused by the refusal of many enterprises to fire workers they do not need.
Since they are not generating enough income, these firms are forced to pay typically low wages late.

Although they have grumbled loudly about the situation, workers have so far been reluctant to engage in mass protests -- much to the disappointment of Russia's communists and their allies, who dominate the parliament.
Workers have relied on relatives, small garden plots, jobs on the side and other means to put food on the table while receiving irregular salaries.
Union leader Shmakov has claimed that 15 million people took place in a day-long strike and protest in November, but the numbers appeared to be exaggerated.
He said on Wednesday that the non-payment of wages had since worsened, and warned that open-ended strikes might take place in the future if the situation did not improve.
